summary: This memo defines one authentication protocol and one privacy protocol for SNMPv2 so management messages can be authenticated and encrypted. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC adds security to SNMPv2, the protocol used to manage network devices. It defines one way to prove that a management message really came from the party that sent it, and one way to hide the contents of that message from anyone listening. Both rely on a key shared between the two ends.

questions: what is the digest authentication protocol
subtitle: How SNMPv2 management messages were made authentic, and optionally secret, with digests and one shared key.

tldr.problem: Management messages travel over ordinary connectionless networks, so an attacker could alter them, replay them or pretend to be a manager, and anyone listening could read the values inside.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a Digest Authentication Protocol that puts a 128-bit MD5 digest and two timestamps in each message, and a Symmetric Privacy Protocol that encrypts the authenticated message with DES in Cipher Block Chaining mode.
tldr.outcome: Both protocols depend on shared secrets and loosely synchronized clocks, which the RFC handles with a responsible management station and a defined initial configuration. The RFC Editor index lists its status as Historic, and no later RFC obsoletes it.

facts.label: Privacy algorithm
facts.value: DES in Cipher Block Chaining mode

facts.label: Private privacy key
facts.value: 16 octets: 8-octet DES key and 8-octet initialization vector

today: RFC 1446 is an April 1993 standards-track memo that the RFC Editor index lists as Historic. No later RFC obsoletes it, so it is kept here as a record of the security protocols defined for SNMPv2.

sections.title: The Threats SNMPv2 Security Has to Meet
sections.content:
The principal threats against which any SNMPv2 security protocol should provide protection are modification of information, the danger that some party alters an in-transit message generated by an authorized party so as to effect unauthorized management operations, including falsifying the value of an object, and masquerade, the danger that a party attempts management operations it is not authorized for by assuming the identity of another party that has the appropriate authorizations. Two secondary threats are also identified, and the protocols do protect against them: message stream modification, where messages are maliciously re-ordered, delayed or replayed further than natural network operation would cause, and disclosure, the danger of eavesdropping on the exchanges between managed agents and a management station.

Two threats need no protection. Denial of service attacks need not be addressed, because such attacks are in many cases indistinguishable from the network failures any viable management protocol must cope with anyway. Traffic analysis need not be addressed either, because many traffic patterns are predictable and protecting against it offers no significant advantage.

The goals follow from the threats: the protocol should verify that each received message has not been modified in transit, verify the identity of the originator, provide that the apparent time of generation of each received message is recent, and, when necessary, protect the contents of each message from disclosure. Three constraints apply. When the requirements of effective management in times of network stress conflict with those of security, the former are preferred. Neither the protocol nor its mechanisms should depend on the ready availability of other network services such as the Network Time Protocol or secret and key management protocols. And a security mechanism should entail no changes to the basic SNMP network management philosophy.

Three security services realize the goals: data integrity, data origin authentication and data confidentiality. The protocols require both data integrity and data origin authentication at all times, because neither is possible without the other, and there is no provision for confidentiality without both.
sections.plainLanguage: The main dangers are someone changing a management message in flight, someone pretending to be a manager, and someone replaying an old message. The RFC also says plainly which dangers it does not try to stop, such as flooding a device with work until it gives up.

sections.title: The SNMPv2 Party
sections.content:
A SNMPv2 party is a conceptual, virtual execution context whose operation is restricted, for security or other purposes, to an administratively defined subset of all possible operations of a particular SNMPv2 entity. A SNMPv2 entity is the actual process that performs network management operations by generating or responding to SNMPv2 protocol messages, and every entity maintains a local database of all parties known to it. Each party is by definition associated with a single authentication protocol and a single privacy protocol, and this memo defines one such authentication protocol and one such privacy protocol.

A party is represented by an ASN.1 value with a partyIdentity, a partyTDomain, a partyTAddress, a partyMaxMessageSize, a partyAuthProtocol, a partyAuthClock, a partyAuthPrivate, a partyAuthPublic, a partyAuthLifetime, a partyPrivProtocol, a partyPrivPrivate and a partyPrivPublic. For the protocols defined here, several of these take on a specific meaning: the authentication protocol names a combination of the Digest Authentication Protocol with a particular digest algorithm, the authentication clock is the party's notion of the current time, the private authentication key is the secret value the digest protocol needs, the public authentication key is a public value the protocol does not otherwise use, the lifetime is an administrative upper bound on acceptable delivery delay, and the privacy protocol and the private and public privacy keys play the same roles for the privacy protocol.

Three message shapes build on the party's ASN.1 value. A SNMPv2 management communication, SnmpMgmtCom, carries a destination, a source, a context and a protocol data unit. An authenticated management communication, SnmpAuthMsg, adds an authentication information part, whose detailed meaning is specific to the authentication protocol in use and has no effect on application semantics. A private management communication, SnmpPrivMsg, carries a privacy destination and a privacy data part holding the possibly encrypted serialization of an authenticated management communication.
sections.plainLanguage: A party is a named identity with its own keys, its own clock and its own rules for how long a message stays valid. Every SNMPv2 message is built in three layers: the plain management request, the authenticated version of it, and the encrypted version of that.

sections.title: The Digest Authentication Protocol
sections.content:
The Digest Authentication Protocol verifies both the integrity of a received message, that is, that the message received is the message sent, and the origin of the message, that is, the reliable identification of the originator. Integrity is protected by computing a digest over an appropriate portion of the message, computing it at the originator, sending it with the message, and verifying it at the recipient. Origin is established because a secret value known only to the originator and the recipient is prefixed to the message before the digest is computed, so the origin is known implicitly when the digest verifies.

To generate a message, the entity looks up the authentication clock and the private authentication key of the originating party and the authentication clock of the receiving party, sets the source timestamp to the source clock and the destination timestamp to the receiver's clock, and then temporarily sets the authentication digest field to the private authentication key. The message is serialized and a digest is computed over the resulting octet sequence. The computed value is placed in the digest field, and the resulting authenticated message is then encapsulated according to the privacy protocol.

To receive a message, the entity extracts the timestamps and the digest, looks up the clock, key and lifetime of the originating party, and rejects the message as unauthentic if the source timestamp plus the lifetime is less than the authentication clock. It then rebuilds the message with the digest field replaced by the private authentication key, serializes it and computes a digest, and rejects the message if that digest does not equal the one received. The RFC notes that great care is needed in reconstructing the serialized value, and that implementations may find it useful to keep a copy of the original and change only the octets that correspond to the digest field.

Rejected messages are counted: a wrong authentication information type increments snmpStatsBadAuths, a message outside the lifetime increments snmpStatsNotInLifetimes, and a mismatched digest increments snmpStatsWrongDigestValues. A message that fails authentication is noted and discarded without further processing. When a message is accepted, the recorded clocks of both parties are advanced to the timestamps it carried.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message carries a fingerprint of itself, computed with a secret key that only the two ends share. The receiver does the same computation with the same key and compares. If the fingerprints differ, the message was changed on the way, and the receiver throws it away and counts the failure.

sections.title: The Symmetric Privacy Protocol
sections.content:
The Symmetric Privacy Protocol protects a received message from disclosure by encrypting an appropriate portion of it with a secret key known only to the originator and the recipient. It assumes a symmetric encryption algorithm, and the message to be encrypted must already be protected according to the Digest Authentication Protocol: only authenticated messages may be protected from disclosure. To generate a message, the entity looks up the private privacy key of the receiving party, serializes the authenticated message and encrypts the resulting octet sequence, which becomes the privacy data. To receive a message, the entity looks up its own private privacy key and decrypts the privacy data, after which normal processing continues.

The RFC fixes particular algorithms to guarantee interoperability, while leaving the protocol itself independent of the choice. For data integrity the choice is MD5: a 128-bit digest is calculated over the designated portion of the message, the use of this algorithm with the Digest Authentication Protocol is identified by the object identifier v2md5AuthProtocol, the private authentication key of such a party is 16 octets, and the authDigest component is 16 octets. For data confidentiality the choice is the Data Encryption Standard in Cipher Block Chaining mode, identified by the object identifier desPrivProtocol. The private privacy key is 16 octets, of which the first 8 octets are the DES key and the second 8 octets are a DES initialization vector. The 64-bit DES key in those first 8 octets is a 56-bit quantity plus 8 parity bits, arranged so that one parity bit is the least significant bit of each octet, and the setting of the parity bits is ignored.

The length of the octet sequence to be encrypted must be an integral multiple of 8, and the data should be padded at the end as necessary, with the actual pad value being insignificant. If the length of an octet sequence to be decrypted is not an integral multiple of 8, the processing should be halted and an appropriate exception noted, and the padding should be ignored after decrypting. The authentication timestamp has a granularity of 1 second.
sections.plainLanguage: To hide a message, the sender encrypts the authenticated message with a key both sides share, and the receiver decrypts it with the same key. The RFC picks MD5 for the fingerprint and DES for the encryption, and fixes how the key is laid out.

sections.title: Clock and Secret Distribution
sections.content:
Both protocols assume the existence of loosely synchronized clocks and shared secret values, and three requirements constrain how those are distributed. If the value of an authentication clock is decreased, the private authentication key must be changed concurrently, because messages sent with a timestamp between the old and new clock value could otherwise be replayed. The private authentication and privacy keys must be known only to the parties that need them, and the secrets should be changed immediately after configuration so that their actual value is known only to the software. And there must exist at least one SNMPv2 entity that assumes the role of a responsible management station, responsible for ensuring that all authentication clocks are synchronized and for changing the secret values when necessary.

Initial configuration of a device has to be done manually: a person must physically visit the device and enter the initial secret values for at least its first secure party. When MD5 is used the initial authentication secret is 128 bits long, and when DES is used an additional 128 bits are needed, 64 bits each for the key and the initialization vector, so these values have to be recorded on a medium in order to be transported. The recommended procedure is to configure a small set of initial parties, one pair of which may be used to configure all the other parties.

The minimal useful set includes one party for the responsible management station and one for the managed agent for each of three combinations: no authentication and no privacy, the digest mechanism with no privacy, and both the digest and the symmetric privacy mechanisms. The last of these can be used to create all other parties. The MIB document supporting these protocols specifies 6 initial party identities, and implementations that do not support a privacy protocol need only the 4 initial parties whose privacy protocol is noPriv. To limit exposure, the responsible management station should change these values as its first operation upon completing the initial configuration, and it must synchronize the authentication clock values for each party it shares with each managed agent.

To verify a secret change when no response arrives, the recommended strategy is to set the public value corresponding to the secret being changed to a recognizable, novel value, so that the responsible management station can retrieve the public value and check whether the change took place.
sections.plainLanguage: The protocol needs a shared secret on both sides and clocks that roughly agree. Someone has to set the first secrets by hand at each device, and then a responsible management station takes over, changing the secrets and keeping the clocks in step.

sections.title: Recommended Practices and Limits
sections.content:
The RFC recommends that a management station discard SNMPv2 responses for which neither the request-id nor the represented management information corresponds to any currently outstanding request, because message duplication is possible. It also recommends not reading an agent's lack of response to an authenticated message as conclusive proof of agent or network failure, since authentication failure traps can be lost or suppressed as a result of clock skew or inconsistent notions of shared secrets.

The lifetime value for a party should be as small as possible, given the accuracy of the available clock devices, the relevant round-trip delays and the frequency with which the responsible management station can verify all clock values, because a large lifetime increases the vulnerability to malicious delays. When sending state-altering messages, a management station should delay each successive message until a positive acknowledgement arrives or the previous message expires, and the managed object snmpSetSerialNo is defined to ensure that set operations are processed in a specific order.

The frequency with which secrets should be changed is indirectly related to the frequency of their use, because frequent use of a secret provides a continued source of data that may help a cryptanalyst, and frequent changes avoid that. Changing a secret after each use is generally regarded as the most secure practice, but carries significant overhead, and in a local environment the threat of disclosure may be insignificant.

For the greatest degree of security, a management station must support constrained, pairwise sharing of secrets as its default mode of operation. Because the protocols use symmetric cryptography, the secrets of a party must be known to all other parties it may communicate with, and as the number of places where secrets are known grows, so does the likelihood and the impact of disclosure. Moreover, if more than two entities know a particular secret, data origin cannot be reliably authenticated, because it is impossible to determine which of them originated a given message. The greatest degree of security is therefore afforded by configurations in which the secrets for each party are known to at most two protocol entities.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC gives a set of habits for running the protocol safely: keep message lifetimes short, change secrets often, and let each secret be known to no more than two devices. That last rule is what makes it possible to tell who really sent a message.

fields.desc: The digest computed over the message with the private authentication key substituted for this field.

fields.desc: The time of generation according to the clock of the party that is to receive the message.

fields.desc: The time of generation according to the clock of the party that originated the message.
